## Goals

- Define the empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) of a network and derive
  the training dynamics of the outputs under gradient flow.
- Explain why, in the NTK parametrization, the kernel of a very wide network
  is deterministic at initialization and hardly changes during training.
- Connect a trained wide network to kernel regression with the NTK, and
  name what is lost in this "lazy" regime.
- Compute and compare kernels with `glassnn.analysis.empirical_ntk` and
  `Linear(parametrization="ntk")`.

## Theory

### Linearization and the tangent kernel

Write $f(x; \theta) \in \R$ for the output of a network with parameters
$\theta \in \R^P$. Around the initial parameters $\theta_0$,

$$
f(x; \theta) \approx f_{\text{lin}}(x; \theta) = f(x; \theta_0)
+ \nabla_\theta f(x; \theta_0)^\top (\theta - \theta_0) ,
$$ {#eq-linearization}

a model that is *linear in the parameters* with the feature map
$x \mapsto \nabla_\theta f(x; \theta_0)$. The kernel of this feature map is
the (empirical) neural tangent kernel [@jacot2018neural]

$$
\Theta(x, x') = \nabla_\theta f(x; \theta)^\top \nabla_\theta f(x'; \theta),
\qquad K = J(X) J(X)^\top ,
$$ {#eq-ntk}

where row $i$ of the Jacobian $J(X) \in \R^{n \times P}$ is
$\nabla_\theta f(x_i)^\top$. $K$ is symmetric and positive semi-definite.

### Training dynamics of the outputs

Take the squared loss $\mathcal L(\theta) = \frac{1}{2n}\lVert f(X) - y\rVert^2$
and gradient flow $\dot\theta = -\nabla_\theta \mathcal L
= -\frac1n J(X)^\top (f(X) - y)$. By the chain rule the outputs move as

$$
\frac{d}{dt} f(X) = J(X)\, \dot\theta = -\frac1n K_t\, (f(X) - y) ,
$$ {#eq-ntk-dynamics}

and the output at any other point as
$\frac{d}{dt} f(x) = -\frac1n \Theta_t(x, X)(f(X) - y)$. In general the
kernel $K_t$ changes with $\theta_t$. If it stays equal to $K_0$, the
equation is linear and solved by

$$
f_t(X) = y + e^{-K_0 t/n} \bigl(f_0(X) - y\bigr),
\qquad
f_t(x) = f_0(x) - \Theta_0(x, X)\, K_0^{-1} \bigl(I - e^{-K_0 t / n}\bigr)
\bigl(f_0(X) - y\bigr) .
$$ {#eq-ntk-solution}

As $t \to \infty$, $f_\infty(x) - f_0(x)$ is the kernel regression
(interpolation) of the residuals $y - f_0(X)$ with the kernel $\Theta_0$:
the trained network is a kernel machine, with all the tools of the
kernel lectures. The eigenvectors of $K_0$ with large eigenvalues are
learned first (compare early stopping, @eq-early-stopping). In discrete
time with learning rate $\eta$, the step $f \leftarrow f - \frac{\eta}{n}
K_0 (f - y)$ is stable if $\eta < 2n / \lambda_{\max}(K_0)$.

### When does the kernel stay fixed? Width and parametrization

Consider one hidden layer of width $m$ in the **NTK parametrization**
(`Linear(parametrization="ntk")`),

$$
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt m} \sum_{j=1}^m a_j \operatorname{relu}(z_j) + c,
\qquad z_j = \frac{w_j^\top x}{\sqrt d} + b_j,
\qquad a_j, w_j, b_j, c \sim \mathcal N(0, 1).
$$ {#eq-ntk-mlp}

The gradient with respect to the output weights is
$\partial f / \partial a_j = \operatorname{relu}(z_j)/\sqrt m$, and similarly
for the other parameters, so the kernel is an *average* over the units:

$$
\Theta(x, x') = 1 + \frac1m \sum_{j=1}^m \operatorname{relu}(z_j)\operatorname{relu}(z'_j)
+ \frac1m \sum_{j=1}^m a_j^2\, \mathbb 1[z_j > 0]\, \mathbb 1[z'_j > 0]
\Bigl(\frac{x^\top x'}{d} + 1\Bigr)
$$ {#eq-ntk-one-layer}

(Exercise 8.1). By the law of large numbers it converges, as $m \to \infty$,
to a deterministic kernel, with fluctuations of order $1/\sqrt m$. During
training each single weight moves by $O(1/\sqrt m)$, so the change of the
kernel is also $O(1/\sqrt m)$, while the output changes by $O(1)$. In the
limit the network trains exactly like its linearization @eq-linearization
[@jacot2018neural; @lee2019wide]. @chizat2019lazy call this *lazy
training* and show that it is not specific to width: any model whose output
is scaled up (and the learning rate down accordingly) behaves the same.

In the **standard parametrization** (PyTorch's default, weights of variance
$\propto 1/n_\text{in}$ and no $1/\sqrt{n_\text{in}}$ factor in the forward
pass), the forward pass at initialization has a similar scale, but the sum in
@eq-ntk-one-layer has no $1/m$: the kernel grows with the width, and a fixed
learning rate becomes unstable for wide networks (Exercise 8.2).

### What the kernel regime does not explain

A network in the lazy regime is a kernel method with a kernel fixed at
initialization: its hidden layers do not learn *features* from the data.
Practical networks of finite width, trained with large learning rates,
leave this regime, and much of their success (for example on images and
sequences, Part III) comes from feature learning. The NTK is the exact
description of one limit, and a useful baseline, not a complete theory of
deep learning.

## Where in the code

::: {.callout-note title="Where in the code"}
`{python} api_link("glassnn.analysis.empirical_ntk")` builds each Jacobian
row from one backward pass, by calling the model on one example at a time
(`{python} src_link("glassnn.analysis._jacobian")`):

```{python}
#| echo: false
show_source("glassnn.analysis._jacobian")
```

and returns $J(X_1) J(X_2)^\top$; the existing `.grad` of the parameters is
saved and restored, so the function can be called in the middle of
training. The cost is $n_1 + n_2$ backward passes and $O((n_1 + n_2) P)$
memory.

The NTK parametrization is an option of `Linear`, whose forward pass
divides the weight by $\sqrt{n_\text{in}}$
(`{python} src_link("glassnn.nn.Linear.forward")`):

```{python}
#| echo: false
show_source("glassnn.nn.Linear.forward")
```

`{python} see_also("glassnn.nn.Linear", "glassnn.analysis.count_parameters", "glassnn.optim.SGD")`
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Differences from PyTorch"}
PyTorch has neither an `empirical_ntk` function nor an NTK option in
`torch.nn.Linear`. The same kernel is computed there with
`torch.func.jacrev` and a matrix product, and the parametrization with a
custom module.
:::

## Try it

The setting of notebook 04: twenty points of $y = \sin(3x)$ in one
dimension, plus a constant second input, and one hidden ReLU layer in the
NTK parametrization.

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import glassnn.functional as F
from glassnn import Tensor, backend, manual_seed, nn, no_grad, optim
from glassnn.analysis import empirical_ntk

backend.set_default_dtype("float64")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.hstack([rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=(20, 1)), np.full((20, 1), 0.5)])
y = np.sin(3 * X[:, :1])
X_grid = np.hstack([np.linspace(-1, 1, 101)[:, None], np.full((101, 1), 0.5)])


def mlp(width, parametrization="ntk"):
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(2, width, parametrization=parametrization),
        nn.ReLU(),
        nn.Linear(width, 1, parametrization=parametrization),
    )


manual_seed(0)
K = empirical_ntk(mlp(100), X).data
print("shape", K.shape, "| symmetric:", np.allclose(K, K.T),
      "| positive semi-definite:", np.linalg.eigvalsh(K).min() > -1e-10)
```

### The kernel at initialization concentrates with width

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for width in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:
    values = []
    for seed in range(10):
        manual_seed(seed)
        values.append(empirical_ntk(mlp(width), X[:2]).data[0, 1])
    ax.plot([width] * 10, values, "o", alpha=0.5)
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("width $m$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\Theta(x_1, x_2)$ at initialization (10 seeds)")
plt.show()
```

### The kernel stays fixed during training of wide networks

Full-batch gradient descent with learning rate 0.5 for 500 steps on
$\frac{1}{2n}\lVert f(X) - y \rVert^2$, for several widths:

```{python}
def train(width, seed=0, steps=500, lr=0.5):
    manual_seed(seed)
    model = mlp(width)
    K0 = empirical_ntk(model, X).data
    K0_grid = empirical_ntk(model, X_grid, X).data
    with no_grad():
        f0, f0_grid = model(Tensor(X)).data, model(Tensor(X_grid)).data
    optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for _ in range(steps):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        (0.5 * F.mse_loss(model(Tensor(X)), Tensor(y))).backward()
        optimizer.step()
    K1 = empirical_ntk(model, X).data
    with no_grad():
        f1_grid = model(Tensor(X_grid)).data
    # The discrete-time version of @eq-ntk-solution with the fixed kernel K0.
    residual, total = f0 - y, np.zeros_like(y)
    for _ in range(steps):
        total += residual
        residual = residual - lr / len(X) * K0 @ residual
    f_lin_grid = f0_grid - lr / len(X) * K0_grid @ total
    change = np.linalg.norm(K1 - K0) / np.linalg.norm(K0)
    return change, f1_grid, f_lin_grid


widths = [10, 100, 1000, 10000]
results = {width: train(width) for width in widths}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(14, 3.2), sharey=True)
for ax, width in zip(axes, widths):
    change, f1_grid, f_lin_grid = results[width]
    ax.plot(X_grid[:, 0], f1_grid, label="trained network")
    ax.plot(X_grid[:, 0], f_lin_grid, "--", label="fixed-kernel prediction")
    ax.plot(X[:, 0], y, "k.")
    ax.set_title(f"m = {width}, kernel change {change:.3f}", fontsize=9)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

The relative change $\lVert K_T - K_0 \rVert / \lVert K_0 \rVert$ falls
roughly like $1/\sqrt m$ (from about 30 % at $m = 10$ to 0.4 % at
$m = 10\,000$). The agreement between the trained network and the
fixed-kernel prediction @eq-ntk-solution becomes systematic only for large
widths: at $m = 100$ the two curves visibly differ, at $m = 10\,000$ they
almost coincide. (At $m = 10$ they happen to be close although the kernel
moves a lot; a single narrow network says little, and notebook 04 averages
over seeds.)

## Exercises

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 8.1: the NTK of one hidden layer"}
Derive @eq-ntk-one-layer from @eq-ntk-mlp by computing
$\partial f/\partial a_j$, $\partial f/\partial c$,
$\partial f/\partial w_j$ and $\partial f/\partial b_j$. Check your formula
against `empirical_ntk` for a network with $d = 3$ and $m = 50$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
$\partial f/\partial a_j = \operatorname{relu}(z_j)/\sqrt m$,
$\partial f/\partial c = 1$,
$\partial f/\partial w_j = a_j \mathbb 1[z_j>0]\, x/\sqrt{md}$ and
$\partial f/\partial b_j = a_j \mathbb 1[z_j > 0]/\sqrt m$. The inner
product of the gradients at $x$ and $x'$ is @eq-ntk-one-layer.

```{python}
d, m = 3, 50
manual_seed(0)
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(d, m, parametrization="ntk"), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(m, 1, parametrization="ntk"),
)
X_check = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=(5, d))
W, b = model[0].weight.data, model[0].bias.data
a = model[2].weight.data[0]
Z = X_check @ W.T / np.sqrt(d) + b
H, D = np.maximum(Z, 0), (Z > 0).astype(float)
K_formula = 1 + H @ H.T / m + ((D * a**2) @ D.T / m) * (X_check @ X_check.T / d + 1)
print(np.abs(K_formula - empirical_ntk(model, X_check).data).max())
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 8.2: the standard parametrization"}
Compute the mean diagonal entry of the empirical NTK at initialization for
widths $m \in \{10, 100, 1000, 10000\}$, once with
`parametrization="standard"` and once with `"ntk"`. What does the result
imply for the largest stable learning rate of gradient descent?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
```{python}
X4 = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(4, 2))
for width in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:
    traces = []
    for parametrization in ["standard", "ntk"]:
        manual_seed(0)
        K4 = empirical_ntk(mlp(width, parametrization), X4).data
        traces.append(np.trace(K4) / 4)
    print(f"m = {width:5d}: standard {traces[0]:9.2f}, ntk {traces[1]:5.2f}")
```

In the standard parametrization the kernel grows linearly with the width
(the gradient with respect to the output weights has $m$ entries of order
1, with no $1/\sqrt m$), while in the NTK parametrization it converges. By
the stability condition $\eta < 2n/\lambda_{\max}(K_0)$, the standard
parametrization needs a learning rate that shrinks like $1/m$, and the NTK
parametrization can use the same learning rate for every width.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 8.3: kernel regression with the NTK"}
Show that for $t \to \infty$, @eq-ntk-solution gives
$f_\infty(x) = f_0(x) + \Theta_0(x, X) K_0^{-1}(y - f_0(X))$. Which kernel
method is this, and what plays the role of the regularization parameter
when training is stopped at a finite time $t$?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}
If $K_0$ is positive definite, $e^{-K_0 t/n} \to 0$, which gives the
formula: kernel ridge-less regression (interpolation) of the residuals
$y - f_0(X)$ with the kernel $\Theta_0$, plus the function at
initialization. At finite $t$, the factor $K_0^{-1}(I - e^{-K_0 t/n})$
damps the eigen-directions of $K_0$ with eigenvalues below about $n/t$,
like a ridge penalty $\lambda \approx n/t$ would: early stopping is the
regularization (@sec-regularization).
:::
